content: It is named after Alessandro Volta, a Lombard physicist (1745–1827), who invented the voltaic pile, recognized as the first modern chemical battery. The volt is defined as the potential difference across a conductor when a current of one ampere dissipates one watt of power. In terms of SI base units, it is expressed as m²·kg·s⁻³·A⁻¹. Alternatively, it can be described as one joule of energy per coulomb of electric charge (J/C). Voltage determines the speed at which electrons move through a circuit. The relationship between voltage and current in devices that obey Ohm's Law is linear. Here are some examples of nominal voltages from various sources: The action potential of a nerve cell is approximately 75 millivolts (mV). A single-cell rechargeable nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) or nickel-cadmium (NiCd) battery has a voltage of 1.2 volts (V). A mercury battery typically has a voltage of 1.355 V. A single-cell, non-rechargeable alkaline battery (e.g., AAA, AA, C, or D cells) has a voltage of 1.5 V. A lithium polymer rechargeable battery has a voltage of 3.75 V. A transistor-transistor logic (TTL) or CMOS power supply operates at 5 V. A PP3 battery, commonly used in small devices, has a voltage of 9 V. An automobile electrical system is nominally referred to as 12 V, but its actual voltage ranges from 11.8 V when discharged to 12.8 V when fully charged, and 13.8–14.4 V while the vehicle is running and charging. Household mains electricity varies by region: 240 V RMS in Australia, 230 V RMS in Europe, Asia, and Africa, 120 V RMS in North America, and 100 V RMS in Japan. Rapid transit systems using a third rail typically operate at 600 to 750 V. High-speed train overhead power lines often operate at 25 kilovolts (kV) RMS at 50 Hz, though exceptions exist. High-voltage electric power transmission lines typically operate at 110 kV RMS or higher, with a record of 1150 kV RMS as of 2005. Lightning voltages vary significantly but are often around 100 megavolts (MV). Note: For sinusoidal signals centered around zero voltage, the peak voltage is √2 times greater than the RMS (root mean square) voltage. Historically, the volt's origins trace back to Alessandro Volta's invention of the voltaic pile in 1800. This invention was partly motivated by a professional disagreement with Luigi Galvani over the nature of galvanic responses. Volta discovered that the most effective combination of dissimilar metals for generating electricity was zinc and silver. In the 1880s, the International Electrical Congress, now known as the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), formally adopted the volt as the unit of electromotive force. At that time, it was defined as the potential difference across a conductor when a current of one ampere dissipates one watt of power. Before the adoption of the Josephson junction voltage standard, the volt was maintained in national laboratories using specially designed batteries called standard cells. In the United States, the Weston cell was used for this purpose from 1905 to 1972.
